overview.body: MASTER unit. Two arrivals close Module 4. First, the coin-flip Destination Gate from Labs 3.x and 4.x retires entirely. A TRIVIA gate replaces it: players answer a TRUE/FALSE question about the city they want to visit, and a wrong answer triggers the same get_redirect detour that the old TAILS branch did. Second, sets arrive as the right tool for tracking unique cities and unique hazards across a game. The trip report grows a TRIVIA section with asked / correct / accuracy stats, and the HAZARDS display uses sorted() on a set to show each unique hazard exactly once.

mentorQuote.quote: The trivia gate is the moment the game stops feeling like a coin-flip simulator and starts feeling like a road trip with friends. Anyone who has driven across Texas knows the deal: someone asks a question about the next stop, you either know it or you get rerouted. We are turning randomness into a small piece of agency. That is what good design feels like: the player earns the next mile.

objectives: Add load_trivia(filename) to function_library.py: parse trivia.txt into a dictionary keyed by city, with each value a list of question/answer dicts
Write trivia_gate(dest, trivia, current, distances) as a lab-local function in lab-4-3.py: ask the player a TRUE/FALSE question about the destination; correct earns it, wrong triggers get_redirect
Replace the coin-flip Destination Gate in the in-game loop with a call to trivia_gate
Build unique_cities = set(visited_cities) and unique_hazards = set(hazards_list) at the start of every game; .add() entries every time a city or hazard is recorded
Replace the post-game 'in' operator uniqueness loop with sorted(unique_cities); replace the .copy().sort() hazard sort with sorted(unique_hazards)
Track trivia_asked and trivia_correct as per-game counters; add a TRIVIA section to the trip report showing asked, correct, and accuracy percentage
overview.keyConceptsText: A set in Python is a collection of unique items with O(1) membership testing. my_set = set() creates an empty set. my_set.add(item) inserts an item (or does nothing if it's already present). len(my_set) gives the unique count. sorted(my_set) returns a new sorted list. Sets are unordered, so iterate them via sorted() for stable display. The trivia data shape introduced this lab is a dictionary keyed by city, with each value a list of dicts: trivia['Austin'] -> [{'question': '...', 'answer': 'TRUE'}, ...]. This combines two patterns from CP2 of Lab 4.1 (dict lookup) and CP2 of Lab 4.2 (list of dicts) into one structure.
overview.textbookReference: Chapter 9 sets section (Programs 9–18 through 9–23) covers set creation, .add(), membership testing, and iteration. sorted() on a set is shown in Program 9–21.

content.body: load_trivia(filename) in the library: it reads trivia.txt into a dictionary of lists. Each city maps to a list of its questions, and each question is a dictionary with 'question' and 'answer' keys. Your game loads it at startup and reports how many questions it found across how many cities.

Trivia is the foundation for the new Destination Gate in CP3. Grouping the questions by city in the loader means the gate can ask trivia['Austin'] and get Austin's questions immediately: parse once at startup, look up forever after.

content.quote: Look at the loaders side by side after this checkpoint: distances return nested dictionaries, city info returns a dictionary of dictionaries, hazards return a list of dictionaries, and trivia returns a dictionary of lists of dictionaries. Each one matches the access pattern the game needs. Pick the shape that makes the consumer code easiest to read.

items: In function_library.py, add a section header comment block titled TRIVIA FUNCTIONS, above the test block at the bottom.
Define load_trivia(filename) with a docstring. Create trivia = {} and open the file.
For each line: parts = line.strip().split(','), then city = parts[0], question = parts[1], answer = parts[2].
If city is not yet a key, set trivia[city] = []. Then trivia[city].append({'question': question, 'answer': answer}).
Close the file and return trivia.
In lab-4-3.py, add TRIVIA_FILE = 'trivia.txt' with your other file constants.
In main(), right after the hazards load, add trivia = function_library.load_trivia(TRIVIA_FILE).
Right after the trivia load, count the questions with an accumulator loop: total_questions = 0, then for city in trivia: add len(trivia[city]) to total_questions.

After the Loaded ... possible hazards. line, print the count. The line is long, so split it into two adjacent f-strings inside one print(): print(f'Loaded {total_questions} trivia questions across ' and, on the next line, f'{len(trivia)} cities.').

content.body: trivia_gate(dest, trivia, current, distances) in lab-4-3.py: instead of a coin flip, the player answers a TRUE/FALSE question about the destination. A right answer earns the trip; a wrong one detours through get_redirect, just like the old TAILS branch. The coin-flip gate retires.

trivia_gate lives in the lab file, not the library. The library holds general-purpose helpers any game could reuse. This function knows this game's banners, its TRUE/FALSE format, and its detour rules, so it stays with the game.

content.quote: This is the heart of the new game feel. The player picks a destination, gets a question, and earns the next leg. Wrong answers are not a punishment; they are a detour, the same way get_redirect rerouted them on a TAILS flip in Module 3. Same mechanical outcome; entirely different feeling at the keyboard.

items: Add import random at the top of lab-4-3.py, with your other imports.
Below the constants, define trivia_gate(dest, trivia, current, distances) with a docstring.
Print the banner block exactly: print(), print('--- TRIVIA TIME! ---'), print(f'To reach {dest}, answer this question:'), print().
Pick a question: q = random.choice(trivia[dest]). Print it indented two spaces, print(f' {q["question"]}'), then print().

Read the answer: answer = function_library.clean_input('TRUE or FALSE? '). Then turn it into a full answer: if answer == 'T' or answer == 'TRUE': set player_answer = 'TRUE'; elif answer == 'F' or answer == 'FALSE': set player_answer = 'FALSE'; else: print('Invalid answer! Counting as wrong.') and set player_answer = 'INVALID', which can never match.
if player_answer == q['answer']: print('CORRECT! You earned your destination.') and return dest, distances[current][dest], True.

else: print(f'WRONG. The answer was {q["answer"]}.'), then the detour, split across two lines: redirect, redirect_miles = function_library.get_redirect( and current, distances, dest). Then print(f'Detour! You ended up going to {redirect} instead.') and return redirect, redirect_miles, False.

In main(), replace the whole coin-flip gate (from print('Flipping to see if Texas cooperates...') through the TAILS branch) with the two calls below, indented to match. Keep the You're headed to and Distance lines that follow, unchanged.
Your gate_result pin was part of the coin-flip gate, so replacing the gate removed it too. Make sure no gate_result line is left.

content.body: Two sets, unique_cities and unique_hazards, filled during play, and sorted() to turn them into the trip report's lists. The hazard section now lists each hazard once, under the title HAZARDS ENCOUNTERED (Unique, A-Z). The Lab 4.2 uniqueness loop and the .copy()/.sort() pattern retire.
A set keeps each value once, automatically. Adding a city you already visited, or a hazard you already faced, changes nothing. That replaces about eight lines of bookkeeping with two.

content.quote: Notice we are building each set from its list, not from set(). On a fresh game the visited list is just ['San Antonio']. On a resumed game, the loaded list might hold several cities, and the set rebuilds with all of them. Both cases handled with one line. That is why set(iterable) exists.

items: At the top of the play-again loop, after the if not resumed_game: block and before the outcome flags, add unique_cities = set(visited_cities) and unique_hazards = set(hazards_list). They are rebuilt every game, including a resumed one.
Everywhere you append to visited_cities, add unique_cities.add(current_city) on the next line. There are two places: arrival at a destination, and the dead-end return to San Antonio.
In the hazard block, right after hazards_list.append(name), add unique_hazards.add(name).

In the trip report block, delete all of the Lab 4.2 bookkeeping: the two sorted_hazards lines (.copy() and .sort()), the unique_cities = [] line, the for city in visited_cities: loop with its if city not in unique_cities: check, and the comments above them. If unique_cities = [] stays, it replaces your set with an empty list. Put sorted_unique_cities = sorted(unique_cities) and sorted_unique_hazards = sorted(unique_hazards) in their place.

In the on-screen hazard section, change if len(sorted_hazards) > 0: to if len(sorted_unique_hazards) > 0:, pass sorted_unique_hazards to display_numbered_list, and change the title to 'HAZARDS ENCOUNTERED (Unique, A-Z)' in both branches, including the no-hazards else branch and its divider. The file written by save_trip_report keeps its own HAZARDS (A-Z): heading.
In the save_trip_report call, pass sorted_unique_cities and sorted_unique_hazards where you passed the old unique-cities list and sorted hazards.

sorted(my_set) returns a new, sorted list. Sets have no .sort() method.
